Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in
message news:3CB5BA56...@white-wolf.com...
> tetragrammaton wrote:
> > Then the ritual of the bitter rose is useless,
> > because there's no blood on the diablerized vampire
> > to be moved.
>
> Since the moving of blood and the burning is handled as
> a unit, this is not true.

But playing RotBR after the diablerie does require counting
the amount of blood that *was* on the burned vampire, since
the vampire's already burned by the time you play it. So
I'm not sure now that it couldn't work the same way if played
in a (hypothetical) divisible diablerie where you played it
after blood-moving at the burn-the-vampire step?

> > > No. RB is played before the Diablerie unit. RotBR is
> > > played after.
> >
> > Are you telling that RoTBR is played *after* the BH vote ?
>
> Yes.

That's kind of icky in that RotBR doesn't look like it should
require surviving the Blood Hunt to be usable, but if it's
played after the BH referendum, a burned vampire can't very
well play it...

All these "play when X" cards seem to produce slightly confusing
timing situations, in that you're supposed to play them 'during'
or 'when' something that's not normally interruptable happens.
(eg Reform Body vs enough aggravated damage to burn: normally you
can't interrupt the "burn blood to prevent destruction" process,
but Reform Body has to be played then, so you do.) Perhaps it'd
be simpler to let them interrupt as appropriate, even during
diablerie, just like Direct Intervention does, and interpret (or
errata) as appropriate for desired functioning?

Josh

When the vamp burns (diablerie), he had blood on him (that
was taken during diablerie). This is not the same effect
if the diablerie is divided into its component steps,
since "at the burning", the vampire has been empty for
a little while.
But since the whole diablerie is treated as a unit, it
works.

> > > > No. RB is played before the Diablerie unit. RotBR is
> > > > played after.
> > >
> > > Are you telling that RoTBR is played *after* the BH vote ?

> (eg Reform Body vs enough aggravated damage to burn: normally you
> can't interrupt the "burn blood to prevent destruction" process,
> but Reform Body has to be played then, so you do.) Perhaps it'd

No. You complete that process, then you play reform body instead of
burning. (i.e., an empty vampire who takes 16 aggravated damage
can play reform body and be saved. He won't have to deal with the
"remaining" aggravated damage because it was all applied - not
interrupted).

> be simpler to let them interrupt as appropriate, even during
> diablerie, just like Direct Intervention does, and interpret (or
> errata) as appropriate for desired functioning?

That'd be a lot of errata to accomplish what the single ruling
does.

> card. Is this indeed when RotBR must be played? Or can it
> be played at the same time Reform Body could have been played?
> If not, why not? And if not, why basically wallpaper a card?

As stated already:
RotBR is played after diablerie.
The Blood Hunt is part of the diablerie.
Reform Body is played before the diablerie.
RotBR cannot be played then since the vampire has not been
burned then. RB is played before the vampire is burned, RotBR
is played after.

Why "wallpaper" the card?
Well, without getting into the point of whether the card is
wallpaper and, if so, it is only because of this ruling that
it is so, the answer is:
To avoid errata. (Some people still hold that less errata is good).

> As stated already:

> burned then. RB is played before the vampire is burned, RotBR

I know you've said this before about the timing of RotBR and
RB, but I don't understand where it comes from. Both use the
exact same timing indication of "being burned". It seems that
you agree that, if diablerie *were* divisible, they'd both be
played at step 3. So why are they played at different points
when diablerie *isn't* divisible? If RB should be played when
the vampire is *about* to be burned, why not play RotBR also
when the vampire is about to be burned? If the motivation is
that RB wouldn't be playable after, since the vampire playing
it wouldn't be in play then, why not apply that motivation
also to RotBR since the diablerist also has a chance of not
being in play after the diablerie?

Josh

Messages.Body:

> I know you've said this before about the timing of RotBR and

> it wouldn't be in play then, why not apply that motivation
> also to RotBR since the diablerist also has a chance of not
> being in play after the diablerie?
>

Er, indivisibility aside, your suggestion would create a strange
situation if we follow the rules that the acting player gets to
play all action modifiers before allowing the reacting player to
play any effects.

Let's have the situation below - with your suggestion being enforced.

A diablerizes Lambach with eight blood on him.
A plays RotBR.

Now one of two situations occur.

1) B screams blood murder as the by now burned Lambach may no longer
react with RB.

2) B happily plays RB after all of A:s vampires have gained the benefit
of RotBR.

I guess a similar effect would be true for Crimson Fury as well, which
in alternative 2 above, if played at inferior, creates a paradox as
all of A:s vampires gain the benefit from the diableri and after that
said diablerie is canceled.

Sten During

"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message

> Joshua Duffin wrote:

> > I know you've said this before about the timing of RotBR and

>
> One would be played instead of the burning (before 3) and the
> other would be played once the vampire is burned (after 3), sure.

The problem I keep running into is, the wording on these
cards indicates that they should be played *during* burning.
It seems to me that we should either allow them to be played
then, in the middle of the "burn this vampire" bit, or reword
them. Just making diablerie indivisible doesn't by itself
take care of these cards; they still need to be "clarified"
or "errataed" to tell us when they should *really* be played,
and what their effects should *really* be.

> The latter's text is just poorly effected errata text which failed to
> preserve the proper original text "if ... vampire is diablerized"
> (which gives a more suitable indication of timing). The errata was
> issued to correct the action modifier *or* combat card usage, not
> to change the timing. [RTR 23-JUN-1998]
>
> I'll correct that wording.

Oh, thanks a lot. ;-)

The original text: "Only usable in combat if an opposing
vampire is diablerized. Each ready vampire you control gains
an amount of blood from the blood bank equal to the amount
of blood on the burned vampire." If we assume this is being
played after the diablerie happens (sensible), then we're
also assuming that RotBR can count the blood that *was* on
the vampire when it was burned. In that case, RotBR isn't
really helped at all by the 'indivisible' ruling; it could
work just as well by counting after (3) the blood that was on
the diablerized vampire before (1) was performed.

> > So why are they played at different points
> > when diablerie *isn't* divisible? If RB should be played when
>
> Before burning or after burning. The burning occurs in the
> indivisible diablerie, so you play the effect before or after,
> as appropriate.

If we're willing to use the phrase "as appropriate", we
don't really *need* an 'indivisible' diablerie to make cards
work as they should. :-)

> If the motivation is to allow RB to be played at all on a
> diablerie, then that motivation is satisfied, since RotBR can
> still be played.

Only now does it occur to me: given that the blood hunt
referendum isn't restricted to "vote-stuff" effects only,
the acting vampire should be able to play RotBR *during*
the blood hunt referendum. Yes?

Josh

You're right, it is weird. But it's not solvable without
rewording at least one of the cards, which was supposed to
be what we were trying to avoid via rulings. :-)

> Let's have the situation below - with your suggestion being enforced.
>
> A diablerizes Lambach with eight blood on him.
> A plays RotBR.
>
> Now one of two situations occur.
>
> 1) B screams blood murder as the by now burned Lambach may no longer
> react with RB.
>
> 2) B happily plays RB after all of A:s vampires have gained the benefit
> of RotBR.

Should be (2) I think. If diablerie were divisible and all
"being burned" effects went "in the middle" of step 3, the
acting Meth would indeed play RotBR first, but the target
Meth would still be able to react with RB "during" the burning.
The weirdness of this - that a bunch of vampires got blood
from a vampire that wasn't burned - really (IMO) ought to be
resolved by rewriting the diablerie section of the rules rather
than errataing/clarifying that RB is played when a vampire is
*about* to be burned and RotBR is played when a vampire *has*
been burned, even though they use the same timing wording.
(which LSJ says ought to be changed for RotBR to reflect its
'original' timing placing it after diablerie; fine, but RB's
text doesn't say "about to be burned" either.)

What I think diablerie's steps should be:

1. Move equipment to the diablerist, move blood to the
diablerist, burn the victim.

Side/after effects:

2. Search library for skill card.
3. Blood hunt referendum, if desired.

Reform Body and Crimson Fury should say "when this vampire is
about to be burned/diablerized" and be played just before (1).
RotBR should say "when this vampire has just diablerized another
vampire" and be played just after (1). (Only (1) is "diablerie"
here.)

That's if I ran the world. :-)

Josh

Joshua Duffin wrote:
> You're right, it is weird. But it's not solvable without
> rewording at least one of the cards, which was supposed to
> be what we were trying to avoid via rulings. :-)

I put much less weight on re-wording existing errata than on creating
new errata for printed material. Especially when the errata'ed wording
doesn't match the stated purpose of the errata, as in the case of
RotBR.

> (which LSJ says ought to be changed for RotBR to reflect its
> 'original' timing placing it after diablerie; fine, but RB's
> text doesn't say "about to be burned" either.)

RB says "is being". Like things you do when someone "is dying",
you do them before (CPR, for instance). That's the nature of "is
verbing" for instant-effect verbs (as opposed to lengthy-effect
verbs, like "is breathing" or "is building"). Contrast "is
adjective" (like "is dead" or "is burned").

You play it at the end. You handle all the damage as part
of damage resolution, even past the point where the vampire has
been torporized or burned. Then, when you're done with damage
resolution (all the damage is handled), the vampire goes to torpor
if he has any unhealed damage (and hasn't been burned).

Otherwise an empty vampire who takes 16 agg damage and plays
Reform Body when he's burned (by the 2nd point) would then
be burned again by the remaining (as yet unhandled) points.

Messages.Author: Raille
Messages.Body:
LSJ wrote:

> Raille wrote:

> > way then immediantly make exceptions.
> >

> > things, especially things that need to be that way, can easily conform

>
> Cards resolve when played (except strikes and actions, by necessity).
> Effects are completely described when played (except political actions).
> Multiple effects are not handled simultaneously (except strikes, by necessity).
>
> Exceptions abound.

Yes they do.

What I'm getting at is that by allowing cards to interact simultaneously
with a *rules section* you still preserve the normal game play of acting
player/reacting player effects. Since the cards still par off with each
player as they get laid on the table, all which is going on during a set
rules section.

This is nothing more than extending the current method of play from a
larger rules section to a small rules section.

Take an action. During the Action multiple effects simultaneously
effect the action. Drop this down a level, and you get the declaration
of an action with allows the acting player to immediantly play card
effects to simulatenously effect that action.

Card is simultaneously played in most cases simply to create the action,
and multiple cards require play as the action is announced.

As you pointed out combat already has this effect built in down to a
finely detailed proceedure.

Why is this simultaneous effect of card to rule section now all of a
sudden prohibited?

Raille
